analysis.title: Weekly Economic Perspectives (October 23, 2026)
key_insights: US housing is deteriorating further. Pending home sales fell 7.3% m/m in September to a record low, and the NAHB homebuilder index fell three points to 29, below the Covid-era low of 30 and the lowest since June 2012.

The 30-year conforming mortgage rate rose from about 6.0% in February to 7.4% in mid-October, worsening affordability. The report says a recent bid in Treasuries may pause the rise but will not give meaningful relief.

The report links the housing weakness to the Fed's 'mini-tightening cycle' and higher mortgage rates. It says housing may get worse before it gets better, while the wider economy keeps growing on consumer spending and AI-related capex.
UK CPI rose 0.4 points to 3.5% y/y in September, driven by petrol and diesel. Core inflation rose to 2.8% and services inflation to 3.7%. Food inflation was steady at 1.6%.

The report expects two 'insurance' Bank of England hikes, in November 2026 and February 2027. It argues the BoE's September signal (vote to hike if energy prices stay high) has been met, and that the BoE's own research says second-round effects become more likely once inflation exceeds 4%.

UK labor data is soft. ILO unemployment fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, though the survey is called unreliable. Payrolls rose 13,000 in September, vacancies keep falling, and private-sector regular pay growth rose from 2.9% to 3.0%, below the pace consistent with 2% inflation.

Japan's September national CPI was 2.148% y/y, just under the report's 2.2% forecast. About 64% of CPI items rose, and the median item rose about 0.2% m/m. Core (ex fresh food) and BoJ core (ex fresh food and energy) each rose 0.5% m/m sa, to 2.1% and 2.4% y/y.

Japanese cost pass-through is broadening. Eating-out sushi prices rose 15.5% y/y while rice prices fell 20.6% y/y, and Teikoku Databank counts more than 8,000 food and beverage products with price increases in September and October alone.

The report's Japan inflation model points to about 2.5% in October and a peak near 3.3% in February. Reaching 2.5% in October needs almost a 1% m/m rise in the headline index, so base effects alone do not explain it.
The report expects a meaningful drop in measured Japanese inflation from April, when the planned food consumption-tax reduction takes effect.
The report expects Japanese Q3 growth to lose considerable momentum. Export values rose 3.3% q/q but export volumes fell 0.4% and import volumes rose 0.8%, so net exports could subtract from growth.

For next week's BoJ meeting the report expects a hawkish hold with higher CPI forecasts and another hike kept on the table. December is a genuine hike risk, but the report is cautious about a rapid sequence of hikes if consumption weakens and inflation falls in spring.

Eurozone flash PMIs diverged. German manufacturing PMI was 54.2 against 53.5 expected, while French manufacturing PMI was 49.3 and French services PMI was 48.4, both below consensus. German ZEW expectations fell to 28.1 from 34.7.

Other releases this week: Canada CPI was 3.1% y/y vs 3.2% expected, UK GfK consumer confidence fell to -24.0 vs -14.0 expected, and UK retail sales ex auto fuel fell 0.4% m/m. US University of Michigan sentiment was 48.0 vs 46.3 expected.
Spotlight on next week: the report expects the Fed to hold at its October meeting, a hawkish-hold from the BoJ, and Australian Q3 CPI of 0.9% y/y.

risk_factors: Mortgage rates keep rising, deepening US housing weakness.
Energy prices stay high, pushing UK headline inflation higher. Oil and gas costs have not fully passed through the economy.
A UK wage-price spiral, which the report says has not started, would be more likely once inflation exceeds 4%.
Japanese inflation near 3% over winter while consumption and growth weaken. The report warns markets may extrapolate the inflation acceleration further than the economy can sustain.
Broad Japanese cost pass-through is reducing household real incomes and encouraging cautious spending.

tension_points.bull_case: Energy-driven CPI at 3.5%, core at 2.8% and services at 3.7%, with more pass-through ahead. The BoE signaled in September it would vote to hike if energy prices stayed high, and the report says that threshold has been crossed.
tension_points.bear_case: Labor market slack and pay growth of 3.0% are below the pace consistent with 2% inflation, and there are few signs of second-round effects so far. The report calls the hikes 'insurance' against a wage-price spiral that has yet to begin.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Not a stated condition. The report says second-round effects become more likely once inflation exceeds 4%.

tension_points.bull_case: Inflation is broadening, with 64% of items rising and a model peak near 3.3% in February. December is a genuine hike risk.
tension_points.bear_case: Consumption is weakening, Q3 growth is losing momentum and food tax cuts from April lower measured inflation, which argues against a rapid sequence of hikes.
tension_points.what_invalidates: If inflation and market pressures stay elevated, December becomes a genuine hike risk. If consumption weakens and inflation turns lower in spring, a cautious pace after any December move is strengthened.

theme_stances.key_argument: The BoE threshold for hiking has been crossed because energy prices stayed high, so two insurance hikes are expected.
theme_stances.evidence: We therefore expect two insurance hikes, in November this year and February 2027

theme_stances.key_argument: Housing may get worse before it gets better given the Fed's mini-tightening cycle and higher mortgage rates.
theme_stances.evidence: The situation may well get worse before it gets better

theme_stances.key_argument: A hawkish hold is expected next week, with December a genuine risk but a rapid sequence of hikes unlikely if consumption weakens.
theme_stances.evidence: we expect a hawkish hold, with higher CPI forecasts and another hike kept firmly on the table
